prompt: Write an essay titled “Anthropic Drops”. It is a finance newsletter column about Anthropic's shares falling in the days after its initial public offering while other artificial-intelligence stocks rallied. About 800 words. Output only the essay, with no title.
raw:
There is an old rule on Wall Street that the market will humiliate whoever is most confident, and that it prefers to do so in public. This week it chose the newest member of the public markets: Anthropic, whose shares have spent the days since their debut drifting steadily downward while nearly everything else with "AI" in its investor deck went up.

The split is strange enough to be worth examining. Chipmakers rallied. Cloud providers rallied. The software companies that spent the past two years explaining how they would "embed intelligence across the workflow" rallied too, some of them sharply. Meanwhile the company that actually builds one of the frontier models those businesses depend on has been marked down, session after session, by investors who were fighting for allocations a few weeks ago.

The easy explanation is that the IPO was priced too richly, and that is probably part of it. Anthropic came to market at a valuation that assumed years of extraordinary growth, and a stock priced for perfection needs only a hint of something short of perfection to fall. When the bankers raised the range and the order book was still oversubscribed many times over, the story was demand. Now the story is supply: early holders, employees with long-awaited liquidity, and fast-money funds that got their allocation and wanted the first-day pop more than a decade of compounding. None of that says anything about the business itself. It is just plumbing.

But plumbing doesn't explain why the rest of the sector went the other way. For that you have to consider what investors actually own when they buy an AI stock, and the uncomfortable answer is that for the past three years the market has mostly rewarded the people selling shovels. Every dollar a model developer spends on training runs and inference capacity becomes a dollar of revenue for someone else, and that someone else usually has thicker margins, a longer operating history, and a balance sheet that does not depend on the next fundraise. When an AI lab goes public, investors see its economics in full for the first time: what it charges, what it spends on compute, and how fast the second number is growing compared with the first. Some of them looked at that and decided they would rather own the companies receiving the cheques.

There is a certain logic to the trade. If you believe AI demand will keep compounding but you're unsure which model will win, the rational move is to buy the infrastructure every contender needs and skip the contenders themselves. The rally in chips and data centers this week is in part a vote of confidence in the whole enterprise, funded in part by selling the one pure-play lab that just became available to sell.

That leaves the other question, the one Anthropic's own management would surely rather discuss: whether the market is mispricing a durable franchise. The bull case has not changed. The company has built a substantial enterprise business, particularly in coding and agentic tools, where its customers tend to be large, sticky, and willing to pay for reliability. Its emphasis on safety, which skeptics once treated as a branding exercise or a competitive handicap, has turned out to matter to exactly the kind of corporate buyers who sign multiyear contracts. Revenue growth, by any ordinary standard, has been remarkable.

The bear case hasn't changed either, and it is now public. Frontier model development is staggeringly capital-intensive. The competitive gap between leading labs is measured in months rather than years. Prices for a given level of capability keep falling, which is wonderful for customers and less wonderful for anyone trying to model terminal margins. And a lab's most important assets, its researchers, can leave in the elevator every night. Private investors could wave these risks away with a long time horizon and a strategic rationale. Public investors have quarterly earnings calls and less patience.

What this week really shows is that the market has started to discriminate. For a long stretch, AI enthusiasm was a rising tide, and almost any company that could tell an AI story saw its multiple expand. A sector where one prominent name falls while its suppliers and customers rise is a sector where investors are finally asking who captures the value, not just whether value exists. That is healthy, even if it is painful for anyone who bought at the open.

It is also worth remembering how little a week tells you. Plenty of companies that later defined their industries spent their first months as public companies underwater, mocked for overreaching at the IPO. Plenty of others that soared on debut never saw those prices again. The early trading of a newly listed stock mostly measures how the deal was structured and who received shares, not what the business will be worth in five years.

For now, the lesson is a modest one. Building the most impressive technology and owning the most profitable position in a value chain are different achievements, and public markets are going to insist on knowing which one they are paying for. Anthropic will have many quarters to make its case. This week the market simply made clear that it will need to.
